heard: The moon's brightest rocks are too young to exist. Apollo astronauts brought back samples of anorthosite, a highly reflective, coarse-grained rock covering the lunar highlands. Scientists believe the entire moon once had a global magma ocean, where these light crystals floated to the top. To study this primordial crust, geologists compared it to similar rock deposits in Canada and Scandinavia. But a 2011 study redated lunar sample 60,025 to just 4.36 billion years old. This young age shattered the theory of a single, rapidly cooling global magma ocean. Now, scientists are debating whether the moon's crust actually built up slowly through multiple volcanic episodes. To solve how planets form, we first have to explain why the moon's brightest rocks are too young to exist.
